title: const and constexpr
summary: `const` means "this value never changes after it is set". `constexpr` means "this value is known **while compiling**". Use them wherever you can: they prevent mistakes and cost nothing.
markdown:
## `const`: a locked box Most values in a program never need to change after they are set. Marking them `const` lets the compiler enforce that. ```cpp const double gravity{ 9.81 }; gravity = 10.0; // error: you cannot assign to a const variable ``` ``` ┌──────────────┐ │ 9.81 │ gravity (locked: read only) └──────────────┘ ``` Two rules: - A `const` variable must be given its value when it is created. - That value may come from anywhere, including the keyboard. It simply cannot change afterwards. ```cpp int age{}; std::cin >> age; const int ageNextYear{ age + 1 }; // set once while running, then locked ``` > [!tip] Make things `const` by default > When you read `const` on a variable, you know its value at every later line without checking. In a long function that is a real help. Leave `const` off only when the value has to change. ## `constexpr`: worked out by the compiler Some values are known before the program ever runs: the number of seconds in a day, the size of a chess board. `constexpr` asks the compiler to calculate them during the build. ```cpp constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; constexpr int secondsPerDay{ 24 * 60 * 60 }; // the compiler stores 86400 int x{}; std::cin >> x; constexpr int bad{ x * 2 }; // error: x is not known while compiling ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph CT["While compiling"] A["constexpr int s{ 24 * 60 * 60 }"] --> B["86400 is written
straight into the program"] end subgraph RT["While running"] C["const int a{ input + 1 }"] --> D["worked out during the run,
then locked"] end ``` You will hear these two phases called **compile time** and **run time**. The distinction comes up again and again in C++. | | `const` | `constexpr` | |---|---|---| | Can change after it is set | No | No | | Value may come from input while running | Yes | No | | Calculated during the build | Sometimes | Always | | Use it for | Any value you will not modify | True constants: `pi`, `maxPlayers`, `gridSize` | ## `constexpr` functions A function can be `constexpr` too. That means the compiler **may** run it during the build when its arguments are known. ```cpp #include constexpr int square(int n) { return n * n; } int main() { constexpr int a{ square(5) }; // worked out while compiling: 25 int side{}; std::cin >> side; int b{ square(side) }; // the same function, used while running std::cout << a << ' ' << b << '\n'; return 0; } ``` One function serves both purposes. ## Replace magic numbers with names A **magic number** is a bare number in the code with no explanation. ```cpp total = price * 1.08; // what is 1.08? ``` ```cpp constexpr double salesTaxRate{ 0.08 }; total = price * (1.0 + salesTaxRate); ``` The second version explains itself. And when the rate changes, you change one line instead of hunting for every `1.08`. ## Sharing constants between files Constants that several files need go in a header, grouped under a name: ```cpp // constants.h #pragma once namespace constants { inline constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; inline constexpr int maxPlayers{ 4 }; } ``` Any file that includes the header writes `constants::pi`. Take the `namespace` and `inline` parts on trust for now. Both are explained in Milestone 3: [[3.05 Scope, Lifetime and Namespaces]] and [[3.06 Global Variables, static and Linkage]]. ## `const` parameters A parameter can be `const` as well: the function promises not to change it. ```cpp void printPrice(const double price) ``` For a simple value that is copied anyway, this is optional. It becomes important with references, where it means "I will look at your data but not alter it": [[4.03 References]]. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Can a `const` variable get its value from user input? - No, a `const` must be known while compiling + Yes, it is set once while running and cannot change afterwards - Yes, and it can be changed again later with another `std::cin` - Only if it is also `constexpr` > `const` only means "cannot change after it is set". It is `constexpr` that needs a value known while compiling, so it cannot come from input. ? What is a magic number? - A number the compiler works out during the build - A number too large for an `int` + An unexplained number written directly in the code - A random number chosen at run time > A magic number is a bare value like `86400` with no name. Replace it with a named constant such as `secondsPerDay`. ? What is the difference between compile time and run time? - They are the same; the program is built as it runs + Compile time is while the program is being built; run time is while it is running - Compile time is how long the build takes; run time is how long the program takes - Compile time happens after run time, when the program finishes > Compile time is while the compiler builds the program. Run time is while the finished program runs, which is when user input arrives. ? Does a `constexpr` function always run during the build? - Yes, that is exactly what `constexpr` means - No, it never runs during the build - Yes, unless it has no parameters + No; only when its arguments are known while compiling > A `constexpr` function *can* run while compiling. With values only known while running, it runs like any other function. ```
ideas:
1. Create `constexpr` constants for minutes per hour, hours per day and days per week. Compute seconds per week from them as another `constexpr`.
2. Try to modify a `const` variable and read the error.
3. Write `constexpr int cube(int n)` and use it once with a literal and once with a value read from the keyboard.

cards.q: Can a `const` variable get its value from user input?
cards.a:
Yes, it is set once while running and cannot change afterwards

`const` only means "cannot change after it is set". It is `constexpr` that needs a value known while compiling, so it cannot come from input.

An unexplained number written directly in the code

A magic number is a bare value like `86400` with no name. Replace it with a named constant such as `secondsPerDay`.

cards.q: What is the difference between compile time and run time?
cards.a:
Compile time is while the program is being built; run time is while it is running

Compile time is while the compiler builds the program. Run time is while the finished program runs, which is when user input arrives.

cards.q: Does a `constexpr` function always run during the build?
cards.a:
No; only when its arguments are known while compiling

A `constexpr` function *can* run while compiling. With values only known while running, it runs like any other function.
